body: {"total":6,"records":[{"title":"Preoperative anaemia clinics before elective hip and knee replacement: an evaluation of referral-to-surgery pathways in four hospitals","authors":"Hallorann-Obi P, Castellanos-Weir J, Nakamura-Dube S","year":2019,"venue":"Perioperative Service Reports","doi":"10.5555/jpms.2019.0162","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We evaluated preoperative anaemia pathways in four hospitals performing elective hip and knee replacement. Of 2,310 patients screened, 17 percent were anaemic. A referral to the anaemia clinic was made for 61 percent of anaemic patients, and the median time from referral to intravenous iron was 19 days. Surgery was postponed for 14 percent of referred patients. Hospitals that screened at the surgical listing visit referred more patients in time than those that screened at pre-assessment. Referral criteria, clinic leadership and data recording differed between the four hospitals, which limited comparison."},{"title":"Screening timing and the window for iron therapy before arthroplasty","authors":"Lindqvist-Amadi R, Pereira-Holt K","year":2021,"venue":"Preoperative Pathway Reports","doi":"10.5555/apcr.2021.0093","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared two screening points for anaemia before elective hip and knee arthroplasty in one health region. Screening at the surgical listing visit took place a median of 84 days before surgery, and screening at pre-assessment a median of 23 days before. Among anaemic patients, 78 percent of those screened at listing received treatment before surgery, against 41 percent of those screened at pre-assessment. Earlier screening identified more patients whose anaemia resolved without treatment, which increased repeat testing. The comparison was observational and the two screening points were used in different hospitals."},{"title":"Referral triggers for preoperative anaemia management: haemoglobin and ferritin thresholds used across orthopaedic centres","authors":"Mbatha-Kowalski E, Ruiz-Ferreira A","year":2016,"venue":"Orthopaedic Service Organisation","doi":"10.5555/oso.2016.0021","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We asked 64 orthopaedic centres which laboratory values triggered referral for preoperative anaemia management. Haemoglobin thresholds ranged from 120 to 130 g/L, and 22 centres used the same threshold for women and men. Ferritin thresholds for iron deficiency ranged from 30 to 100 micrograms per litre, and 18 centres did not test ferritin routinely. Only 11 centres had a written pathway naming who would act on an abnormal result. The response rate was 58 percent, and centres with an established pathway may have been more likely to reply."},{"title":"Patients' experiences of a preoperative anaemia pathway: travel, infusions and postponed surgery","authors":"Okafor-Brennan T, Sato-Lindgren H","year":2023,"venue":"Perioperative Patient Experience","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We spoke with 22 patients referred to a preoperative anaemia clinic before joint replacement. Many did not understand why a blood result could delay their operation and felt they had been sent back to the end of the queue. Patients living far from the hospital described long journeys for a short infusion and asked for treatment closer to home. Several valued a named nurse who explained the plan. Patients whose surgery was postponed reported more pain and worry during the wait. Participants came from one hospital and were invited by the clinic nurse."},{"title":"Organisational models of perioperative anaemia services: a scoping review","authors":"Achterberg-Nkemelu D, Harcourt-Ito M, Vasquez-Salo B","year":2022,"venue":"Perioperative Service Design Review","doi":"10.5555/psdr.2022.0118","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We charted 41 reports of perioperative anaemia services across surgical specialties. Services were led by anaesthetists in 19 reports, haematologists in 9, specialist nurses in 8 and general practitioners in 5. Only 14 reports described the referral pathway in enough detail to reproduce it, and 9 reported waiting times from referral to treatment. Orthopaedic services were the most common setting. Few reports described how patients living far from the hospital received intravenous iron. The authors call for standard reporting of pathway steps and times."},{"title":"Intravenous iron before elective joint replacement and perioperative transfusion: an observational comparison","authors":"Grieve-Adeyemi L, Moreau-Nakashima R","year":2018,"venue":"Preoperative Pathway Reports","doi":"10.5555/apcr.2018.0047","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In 1,140 anaemic patients undergoing elective hip or knee replacement, perioperative transfusion was required in 9.8 percent of those who received intravenous iron before surgery and 15.2 percent of those who did not. Patients who received iron had surgery a median of 12 days later. Treatment was not allocated at random, and patients treated with iron had lower haemoglobin at screening but were younger and had fewer comorbidities. The authors note that the time needed for treatment was the main operational barrier."}]}
